extracted.intended_audience: general readers; aspiring poets and scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on what makes a poet and the poet's work: what to observe, know, and aim for in poetic composition and the scholarly life that supports it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality over imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: No man was ever great by imitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson (through Imlac) argues that imitation cannot produce greatness. A poet should not rely on copying predecessors but must attend to nature and life to create original work: "My desire of excellence impelled me to transfer my attention to nature and to life."

rubrics_metrics.name: Make nature and life your subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature was to be my subject, and men to be my auditors. I could never describe what I had not seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet must draw from direct observation: mountains, deserts, rivers, plants, animals, minerals, and meteors all supply images. Johnson stresses that a poet 'could never describe what he had not seen' and thus must range widely in the world to collect material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Store the mind with inexhaustible variety
rubrics_metrics.description: To a poet nothing can be useless. Whatever is beautiful and whatever is dreadful must be familiar to his imagination; he must be conversant with all that is awfully vast or elegantly little.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect images from every domain—gardens, woods, rocks, skies, and human life—to provide material for enforcement or decoration of moral or religious truth. The poet's power of diversifying scenes and supplying remote allusions depends on this breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to species & prominent features rather than minutiae
rubrics_metrics.description: This business of a poet is to examine, not the individual, but the species; ... He is to exhibit in his portraits of nature such prominent and striking features as recall the original to every mind, and must neglect the minuter discriminations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and present broad, recognizable features and general properties that evoke the original for many readers, rather than obsessing over tiny, idiosyncratic details that will not register universally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand all modes of life and the human condition
rubrics_metrics.description: He must be acquainted likewise with all the modes of life. His character requires that he estimate the happiness and misery of every condition, observe the power of all the passions in all their combinations, and trace the changes of the human mind ... from the sprightliness of infancy to the despondence of decrepitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet should study social institutions, climates, customs, and the variations of human passions so that characters and situations in verse reflect universal truths about human life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divest oneself of local prejudices; seek general and transcendental truths
rubrics_metrics.description: He must divest himself of the prejudices of his age and country; he must consider right and wrong in their abstracted and invariable state; he must disregard present laws and opinions, and rise to general and transcendental truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic judgement should aim for universal insight rather than conforming to contemporary fashions or local biases. Johnson also counsels patience and contempt for immediate praise: commit claims to posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write as interpreter of nature and legislator of mankind (ambition & moral purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: He must write as the interpreter of nature and the legislator of mankind, and consider himself as presiding over the thoughts and manners of future generations, as a being superior to time and place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet's work carries moral and social ambition: strive for works with enduring influence rather than ephemeral approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master languages, sciences, and the delicacies of style
rubrics_metrics.description: He must know many languages and many sciences, and, that his style may be worthy of his thoughts, must by incessant practice familiarise to himself every delicacy of speech and grace of harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical learning (languages, sciences) and sustained practice in diction, cadence, and harmony are essential to give adequate expression to complex thought and imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of early poets: strength & invention vs later elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: It is commonly observed that the early writers are in possession of nature, and their followers of art; that the first excel in strength and invention, and the latter in elegance and refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson notes a critical tendency to privilege ancient poets for vigor and invention; later poets may refine style but risk losing the primal force of natural inspiration—an evaluative distinction to bear in mind when judging poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholar's vocation and practices
rubrics_metrics.description: To talk in public, to think in solitude, to read and to hear, to inquire and answer inquiries, is the business of a scholar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For those pursuing learned composition (including poetic craft informed by learning), maintain a balance of public discourse and private thought, continuous reading and listening, and active questioning and responding as the daily work of intellectual development.
